item.title: Stop Reviewing Pull Requests
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Agentic Coding · Part 5 of 5 · Read the whole series

A provocative paper, on purpose. A position paper in the form of a short scientific paper: a thesis, a model, a simulation, and predictions that could prove it wrong. It follows Review the Intent, Not the Diff, which kept review and changed its object; this paper asks whether we need the review at all. Figures are my own, drawn and simulated with the code in figs.py.

Abstract. Human approval of every pull request became standard when code was written by hand and defects found late were expensive. I model the review gate as an investment that pays when : the chance a change still carries a defect after automated checks, times the share a reviewer catches, times the late-fix cost avoided, must exceed the cost of the gate. Agentic coding shrinks the late-fix cost of most changes, but not where harm survives a revert. The model therefore yields a rule rather than a ban: approve what you cannot undo; watch everything else. Watching means rules in every session and a daily audit of the whole codebase. The approval that remains is a thin gate placed late, at the point of no return, rather than at the merge. In a simulation of a team merging 40 changes a day, the audit and the thin gate together leave a third of today’s latent defects and the same number of irreversible incidents, for about 80 minutes of people time a day instead of 16 hours. I state the conditions under which this holds and five predictions to test it.

TipClaims
  1. The rule. Approve what you cannot undo. Watch everything else.
  2. Why. A gate pays only when . Cheap fixes and fast rollback make small, except where harm survives a revert.
  3. Watching. Rules every session must follow, merge on green, and a daily audit whose report drives the team’s work.
  4. The gate that remains. Thin and late: at the point of no return, a few questions with evidence, rarely needed. It guards the act, not the code.
  5. The condition. Watching beats approving only if the audit reaches far enough and fast enough: .
  6. The test. Teams that adopt the rule should fail no more often and find defects sooner. If they do not, the thesis is wrong.

1. Introduction

For most changes, nobody should have to approve the pull request. The usual answer is that this would end in chaos. I do not think so, and the reason is economic. Review is a control, and every control has a price. We paid it because the gate was the cheapest place to catch a defect: minutes at review against days once it reached users.

Agentic coding changes the price on both sides. Rules can be enforced inside every session instead of at its end. A fix takes an agent minutes, and a flag can switch a change off in seconds. Correction is cheap now, and I believe that is what changes the whole picture. Human attention stays expensive, and the gate spends it on every change, whether or not that change needs it.

Correction is not cheap everywhere. Deleted data, leaked credentials or money sent to the wrong account cannot be taken back by a revert. Hence the rule: approve what you cannot undo; watch everything else. Where approval remains, it must come late and stay small, or it brings little.

2. Background: what review was for

Inspections. Formal code inspection began at IBM in the 1970s as a defect-removal step (Fagan 1976), justified by the claim that a defect costs one to two orders of magnitude more to fix in operation than in development (Boehm 1981). The empirical basis of that curve is thinner than its fame (Bossavit 2015), and agile practice argued that integration and automated tests flatten it (Beck 1999).

What modern review finds. Lightweight review replaced inspections in most teams (Rigby and Bird 2013). At Microsoft, developers named finding defects as their first motivation, yet most comments concerned code improvement and understanding (Bacchelli and Bird 2013); a later study was titled Code Reviews Do Not Find Bugs (Czerwonka et al. 2015). About three quarters of the issues found concern evolvability rather than behaviour (Mäntylä and Lassenius 2009; Beller et al. 2014). At Google, people valued education, norms, gatekeeping and accident prevention most (Sadowski, Söderberg, et al. 2018).

Evidence for review. Components with low review coverage had more post-release defects in three open-source projects (McIntosh et al. 2014), and careful reading improves quality (Kemerer and Paulk 2009). On approval, the largest survey of delivery performance found that external approval slowed delivery without reducing failed changes, and recommended lightweight peer review instead (Forsgren et al. 2018).

Agentic review today. The Claude Code team at Anthropic already lets low-risk changes merge without a person when automated review passes, and reports more merged changes and fewer reverts (Claude Code team, Anthropic 2026). The rule proposed here replaces their risk score with a simpler question and makes no-approval the default.

3. A cost model of the gate

Consider one change. Let be the probability that it still carries a defect after all automated checks; the share of such defects a human reviewer catches; the cost avoided by catching it at review; and the full cost of the gate for one change, including reading, waiting and context switches. The gate pays for itself when

The late cost is the work of the fix plus the harm done while the defect lives. If harm accrues at a rate and the defect is found after a time ,

What agents change. Session rules can lower : an agent can be made to add tests for every changed behaviour, keep coverage of changed lines above a threshold and follow a conventions file, and checks delivered while code is written are the ones developers act on (Sadowski, Aftandilian, et al. 2018). This is not automatic, since code written with AI assistants can be less secure (Pearce et al. 2022; Perry et al. 2023), so the simulation keeps the same under every policy. Meanwhile does not fall: careful review proceeds at a few hundred lines an hour (Kemerer and Paulk 2009), volume rises, and waiting grows roughly as with reviewer utilisation (Kingman 1961).

The main assumption. The term that moves most is . Assumption A: for most defects, an agent can produce a correct fix within an hour of the report, and a flag or a rollback can stop the harm within minutes. Under A, is small, flags cap (Humble and Farley 2010), and an audit caps . Agents resolve a meaningful share of real repository issues under controlled evaluation (Jimenez et al. 2024), and the best teams in Forsgren et al. (2018) already restored service in under an hour; neither measures agent-made fixes in production, so prediction H3 tests A directly.

Where the rule comes from. Assumption A flattens the cost curve only for harm that a revert removes. When harm persists after a revert, stays large however quickly the defect is found, and the gate still pays (the red point in Figure 3). Everything else drifts below the break-even line. The model does not say “never review”; it says exactly where review still pays.

4. The rule in practice

What cannot be undone. A change is a one-way door (Bezos 2016) when its harm survives a revert: data destroyed or exposed, money moved, credentials or signing keys changed, a public interface released outside the team, a message sent to customers. The list is explicit, versioned and part of the session contract. Code that touches it merges like any other; its irreversible step waits at the thin gate (§5). Sessions steered from outside the team belong to the same category: an outsider’s issue or a web page can direct an agent (Greshake et al. 2023), and a planted backdoor or a leaked secret cannot be undone either. The contract records where each session’s instructions came from, so such sessions are flagged automatically.

What watching means. Every change merges on green, and everything that is not a one-way door is released without waiting. It is watched at three points (Table 1): before the merge by a session contract enforced by the agent and CI; after it by flags and monitoring; and once a day by an audit that reads the whole codebase and production signals and writes a short report that the team reads instead of forty diffs. When a problem keeps reappearing, the team turns it into a rule, so the contract gradually absorbs what reviewers used to write in comments.

What the audit sees that a pre-merge check cannot. Fast checks belong in the contract. The audit adds slow checks such as mutation testing and fuzzing, patterns across changes, production signals since yesterday’s merges, and trends people can judge before any rule encodes them. A per-change reviewer misses the second and third kind too.

Table 1. A minimal session contract and audit. Thresholds and exact checks are for each team to set; the split is the point. What can be decided per change is enforced by machines; what needs judgement is batched once a day for people.
Session contract (every change, blocking) Daily audit (whole codebase, advisory)
Tests Tests added or updated for each changed behaviour Mutation score by module, and its trend
Coverage Coverage of changed lines ≥ threshold; total never decreases Untested hotspots: code that changes often and is weakly tested
Integrity No test deleted or assertion weakened without a linked decision Weakened or skipped tests, by session
Conventions Conventions file, linters and types pass Drift from conventions and architecture rules
Intent A change to a contract or invariant updates its decision record Decision records changed since yesterday
Production User-facing behaviour behind a flag Errors and performance since the last merges
One-way doors Listed actions wait at the thin gate; sessions steered from outside are flagged Gate load: share of changes reaching it, minutes per decision

The integrity rule stops the most common failure of coding agents, an agent that edits a test until it passes. Coverage is paired with mutation testing because coverage alone is a weak measure of test quality (Inozemtseva and Holmes 2014) and becomes a target once enforced (Strathern 1997); mutation testing measures whether tests notice a change in behaviour (Papadakis et al. 2019).

Who is accountable. The person who starts a session owns what it merges. Steering the agent and looking at its output is part of writing, and it stays. What disappears is the second person whose approval was required.

Intent changes. The previous essay sent every change of intent to a person before merging. The rule refines that: a change to a contract or invariant that can be reverted merges, but never silently. It updates its decision record, and the team reads it the next morning. Only intent that guards a one-way door meets the thin gate.

5. The thin gate

Where the remaining gate sits and how much it asks decide whether it is worth having. A gate placed early and made thick, with a person reading every diff of every risky change, brings little. A gate placed late and kept thin keeps most of the value that is left.

Late: at the point of no return, not at the merge. Merging is reversible; code that touches a one-way door is safe until it runs. The irreversible act comes later: running the migration, rotating the key, sending the message, turning on the flag that moves money. The gate belongs there. The person judges what will actually run, with real data and configuration; the approval cannot go stale; and the gate holds back one action, not the team.

Thin: a few questions with evidence, not a diff. Reading code is slow, and reviews get shallower as changes grow (Kemerer and Paulk 2009). At the point of no return, five questions suffice (Figure 4). What exactly cannot be undone? What did a rehearsal, such as a dry run on a copy of production, show? What is affected, and can the action be staged? What is the way back, and has it been tested? Who asked, and did any instruction come from outside the team? The agent prepares the answers; the person checks them and chooses to go, to stage the action, or to stop. Staged releases are standard practice when an effect is uncertain (Beyer et al. 2016).

In the terms of Equation 1, a thin, late gate raises , because the person examines evidence about the one thing that matters, lowers , because the decision takes minutes and is rarely needed, and sits where is largest. A thick, early gate does the opposite on all three counts. One case needs more than five questions: a session steered from outside the team, where the danger hides in the code itself. There a person reads the diff or, better, the work is redone in a session the team steers.

Rare: keep it thin on purpose. Gates grow. Every incident adds an item to the list, and a long enough list turns the thin gate back into the old one, approved by tired people who no longer read. Track its load: the share of changes that reach it and the minutes per decision. When the same kind of action keeps arriving, make it undoable instead of adding approvers: soft deletes, schema changes that expand before they contract (Ambler and Sadalage 2006), keys that can be rolled back, releases region by region. Each piece of reversibility moves a class of changes from “approve” to “watch”. The best gate is one with less and less to do.

6. A simulation

I simulated a team under five policies: a gate on every change (today’s common practice), no gate and no audit, an audit alone, the audit with the thin gate (the proposal), and a gate on every change with the audit. Each change may carry a reversible defect; one in twenty also carries an irreversible step, which may itself be defective. A defective irreversible step that runs unstopped is an irreversible incident: the nightly audit comes too late for it. The parameters (Table 2) are chosen rather than measured and, where I had to choose, generous to review.

Table 2. Simulation parameters. The audit includes production signals, so monitoring counts as part of the watch, not as users. The review queue is optimistic for the gate: reviewers start as soon as they are free. A value of is high for functional defects given what review is known to find (Mäntylä and Lassenius 2009; Czerwonka et al. 2015).
Parameter Value

No gate, no audit 0.4 h (0.7 h) 0 19.2 2.0
Gate on every change (today) 1.1 h (4.0 h) 16 h 9.7 1.0

Chaos is real, but it is not the proposal. With no gate and no audit, latent defects double and irreversible incidents double. The critics are right about that policy, not about the alternative.

Each mechanism does one job. The audit alone cuts latent defects to a third of today’s, but leaves irreversible incidents at the chaos level, because a nightly audit finds them after the harm. The thin gate alone brings incidents back to today’s level, for 20 minutes a day. Together they beat today’s practice on reversible defects and match it on irreversible ones, at a twelfth of the people time. If the evidence at the thin gate lets it stop 80% of defective steps instead of 50%, incidents fall to 0.4 a month, well below today’s.

The price of the full gate. Adding a gate on every change to the audit lowers latent defects from 3.3 to 1.6 and does not reduce irreversible incidents, for 16 hours a day: about 10 engineer-hours for every day of latent defects it prevents (16 h ÷ 1.7 ≈ 9.4). Does a latent defect in this part of the system cost more than 10 engineer-hours a day? For a reversible defect in an internal tool, rarely. For a payment flow, easily, and that is a one-way door with its own thin gate.

Speed and reach of the watch. By Little’s law (Little 1961), latent defects equal the rate at which they enter times how long they stay. A gate removes at most the factor , here a half; an audit shortens the stay, here by a factor of six. But the audit may see only a share of defects, the rest being found by users. The proposal then beats today’s practice when

In plain words, the watch must see more kinds of defect than a reviewer would have caught, and the slower it is, the more it must see. With the values of Table 2, an audit that finds what it sees in about two days must see at least 60% of defects, and one that takes five days, 75% (Figure 6). If a team’s defects are mostly of a kind no machine can notice, the rule fails for that team, and Equation 3 says so before any harm is done. Measure first, and where it falls below the bound, keep reviewing changes to that part of the code until the watch improves.

7. Predictions and a test protocol

Speed is not a useful test: removing a gate obviously speeds up merging. The thesis stands or falls on quality and on its assumptions. For teams that adopt the rule, compared with similar teams that keep the gate:

  • H1. No loss of stability. Change failure rate and time to restore service (Forsgren et al. 2018) are no worse, within a margin fixed in advance, and irreversible incidents do not rise.
  • H2. The watch sees far enough. The share of defects found first by the audit or monitoring rather than by users, an estimate of , exceeds the bound of Equation 3, and defects are found sooner.
  • H3. Fixes are cheap (Assumption A). For defects found by the audit, the median time from report to merged fix is under one working hour, and a flag or rollback contains the harm before the fix lands.
  • H4. The report is used. At least half of the audit’s findings are fixed or explicitly dismissed within a week. An audit nobody reads turns the proposal into the chaos case.
  • H5. The gate stays thin. The share of changes reaching the thin gate and the minutes per decision stay small, and fall as more actions are made undoable.

Protocol. In a stepped-wedge design, teams adopt the rule one at a time, in random order, over several months, so every team is observed under both policies and calendar effects are controlled. H1 is a pre-registered non-inferiority test; H2 to H5 and lead time are secondary outcomes, measured from repository, pipeline and incident logs rather than self-reports, since teams cannot be blinded. If H1, H2 or H3 fails, the thesis is wrong for the teams studied.

8. Objections and limitations

“Review demonstrably reduces defects” (McIntosh et al. 2014). Compared with no review, on hand-written code, yes. The relevant comparison is review against watching, which H1 and H2 test. The recommendation of peer review in Forsgren et al. (2018) rests on data that predate agents; extending it is an extrapolation.

“Review is how teams share knowledge” (Bacchelli and Bird 2013; Sadowski, Söderberg, et al. 2018). It was. The replacement is deliberate: decision records, conventions, and a daily report read by the whole team rather than forty diffs each read by one person.

People adapt. Without a reviewer, authors may grow careless, or more careful because they alone own the result. The simulation holds fixed; H1 measures the net effect.

Compliance. Some standards require custom code to be reviewed before release; PCI DSS sets conditions on who may review when the review is manual (PCI Security Standards Council 2022). Whether automated review satisfies them is for auditors to decide; where it does not, the code joins the list of one-way doors.

Loss of skill. Automation leaves people responsible for rare, hard cases while removing the practice that prepares them (Bainbridge 1983). Teams must keep the skill on purpose: reading the audit’s findings in the code, tracing incidents by hand, rotating who does it.

Limits of the model. It is linear and treats defects as independent. It does not weight defects by harm, so if reviewers mainly catch severe ones it is biased against the gate; the irreversible cases, which keep their gate, are meant to cover the worst. It counts the audit as an hour of reading, ignoring its compute cost and false alarms. It holds constant, although reviewers tire and large changes get shallower reviews, and it ignores what reviewers learn. The thin gate’s catch rate is assumed equal to a reviewer’s, not measured. The parameters describe one team at one rate: the direction of the result holds wherever Equation 3 holds, not its magnitude. Finally, the paper assumes writing code is no longer the bottleneck, and the evidence on how much AI speeds up experienced developers is mixed (Becker et al. 2025).

9. Conclusion

The pull request review was the right control while late defects were expensive and a person’s reading was the main check. With agentic coding, rules run inside every session, most defects are cheap to fix the next day, and the one step that has not become faster is the person reading the diff.

What keeps a codebase healthy is how quickly defects are found and how cheaply they are undone, not whether someone looked at each change before it merged. Where harm cannot be undone, a person still decides, late and briefly, at the point of no return: the gate guards the act, not the code. Where a machine cannot see, the team should measure that before it lets go.

This means giving up control of each change. In return, we can simplify our processes instead of adding layers to protect a kind of control that, in the past, was the only kind available. Approve what you cannot undo. Watch everything else.

The views in this paper are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

item.title: Review the Intent, Not the Diff
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Agentic Coding · Part 4 of 5 · Read the whole series

Analysis, October 2026. An analysis of the Claude Code team’s post Solving code review at Anthropic, read in the light of my earlier paper Intent Is the Source. Unless stated otherwise, numbers come from that post. Figures are my own, drawn with the code in figs.py.

The bottleneck moved

Once a team adopts agentic coding, code stops being the bottleneck. Review takes its place. PRs pile up, everyone is nervous to approve them, and the speed you gained writing code is lost waiting for someone to read it.

The Claude Code team at Anthropic, where Claude writes roughly 90% of the code, recently shared how they handled this. Between June and September, their merged PRs more than doubled while the share of reverted PRs fell by over 40%. They did not remove review. They moved most of the reading to machines and pointed human attention at the risk.

Six layers and a classifier

Their approach stacks six layers of checks with fast rollback underneath: verification, required CI, AI review, security review, human approval, and a merge queue with feature flags.

A few principles hold it together:

  1. Review happens before the PR exists. It runs continuously, more like a spellchecker than a gate at the end. By the time a human looks, Claude has usually reviewed and fixed the change at least once.
  2. The agent must prove its work. Tests, a build, or a screenshot compared against the design. It shows output instead of claiming it is done, and a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context.
  3. Risk is assessed per change. A classifier reads the change, not the author, and sets the tier. Low-risk changes merge without a human if automated review passes. Medium risk needs one person, high risk needs two.
  4. Accountability stays human. Whoever prompted a change owns it and counts as a required reviewer. An agent’s approval never replaces a human one.
  5. The reviewer keeps learning. Past incidents become daily evals, noise is measured by how people react to comments, and review rounds are capped so author and reviewer agents converge instead of looping.

It is a thoughtful system, and I largely agree with it.

What the numbers show

The results are strong, but they come from one team measuring itself. Merged PRs can double because changes got smaller, so the count says more about pace than about how much was built. A revert is also only one measure of quality: a bug fixed forward, or switched off behind a flag, never shows up as a revert. What the numbers do show is the claim that matters most. The pace of merges rose sharply and quality, by this measure, improved.

What review quietly did

PR review was never only about catching bugs. It also built a shared understanding of the codebase. Reading each other’s diffs is how teams learned the architecture, absorbed the conventions, and noticed when someone was drifting from them.

That side effect is now mostly gone. Anthropic writes that nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code, “and we don’t think anyone needs to.”

I half agree. Not everyone needs every detail. But the whole team should understand the main architectural patterns, the interfaces and the conventions. Open Slack channels and asking Claude to explain bits of code on demand are useful, but they are not the final answer.

Let go of one more thing

Here is where I would push further. We need to let go of the belief that shared understanding has to come from reading code.

In practice, review served as an accidental knowledge channel. You learned the system as a by-product of checking someone else’s work. That worked when humans wrote every line at human speed. At agentic speed it cannot scale, and trying to preserve it is nostalgia.

We have done this before. Decades ago we stopped reading assembly, yet we still understood our systems, because understanding moved up a level of abstraction. Code is heading the same way.

The comparison has a limit, and it matters. We could stop reading assembly because compilers are deterministic: once we trusted one, it stayed trusted. Agents are not. In Intent Is the Source I called them stochastic compilers, correct only up to their checks. So this climb is safe only if the level above can be checked. Intent written only as prose would not be enough.

The intent layer

Make shared understanding deliberate instead. Humans own the intent: architecture decisions, interface contracts, invariants and conventions. Agents own the implementation. Review checks one against the other.

The intent layer becomes the artifact the team reads, discusses and evolves together. It is short enough that everyone can hold it in their head, and explicit enough that agents can follow it and reviewers can enforce it. Conventions live in agent instructions and linters. Contracts live in typed interfaces and tests. Decisions live in short records that explain the why.

This also tells us when a person must read. A change that only implements existing intent can be checked by machines: the tests pass, the contracts hold, the linters stay quiet. A change that alters the intent always goes to a person, whatever its size. That covers a new contract, a weakened invariant or a reversed decision. It also covers the most common quiet failure of coding agents: an agent that edits a test until it passes has changed the intent, not implemented it.

The same rule keeps the intent layer from drifting, the way design documents usually do. The code is checked against it on every change, and it cannot change unless someone decides it should. Not every part can be checked by a machine. Contracts, invariants and conventions can. Decisions are prose, so the AI reviewer and people check that a change still respects them. The rule fits the Anthropic setup well: their risk classifier could treat any change to the intent layer as high risk by definition.

Where it breaks

Abstractions leak. When an incident hits, someone still has to go deep into the code. That skill fades when nobody uses it, so teams will need to keep it on purpose: incident drills, rotating who traces a bug by hand, reading the code behind a decision record from time to time.

Reading code does not go away. What goes away is the need to read all of it to know how the system works.

Own the why. Delegate the how. Review the intent, not the diff.

Agentic Coding · Part 3 of 5 · Read the whole series

A provocative paper, on purpose. This is a position paper, written to argue one side as strongly as I can, in the form of a short scientific paper. It states a thesis, defines its terms, gives arguments and evidence, and ends with predictions that could prove it wrong. It is not a neutral survey. A follow-up to The Interface Is Data. Figures are my own, drawn with the code in figs.py.

Abstract. Each generation of programming has turned what people used to write into something the machine generates: machine code into the output of assemblers, assembly into the output of compilers, boilerplate into the output of frameworks. I argue that agentic coding, in which a language model plans, edits, runs and repairs code inside a loop, is the next step on this ladder, and a larger one than it looks. The thesis is that the agentic loop is both the next IDE and the next programming language. I define a program as a tuple of intent, executable checks, context and tools, and the agent as a stochastic compiler that is correct only up to the checks. From this definition follow four arguments (historical, structural, economic, empirical), one central consequence (the precision of the new language is the strength of its checks), and four predictions that can be measured within a few years. I end with the strongest objections, including Dijkstra’s, and the evidence that currently cuts against me.

TipClaims
  1. The language. In agentic coding, the source is intent plus executable checks, plus the context and tools the agent may use. Code becomes an intermediate representation: still readable, rarely written.
  2. The compiler. The agent behaves as a compiler that is stochastic rather than deterministic, and correct only up to the checks it is given.
  3. The precision. The new language is exactly as precise as its checks. Tests and types become the type system of intent.
  4. The IDE. The development environment moves from an editor built for typing to a loop built for steering and reviewing: plan, diff, checks, decision log.
  5. The test. These claims predict measurable shifts in how professional software is written. If those shifts do not appear, the thesis is wrong.

1. Introduction

Programming languages are usually described by their syntax and semantics. A more useful description, for the argument here, is what a person has to write and what the machine produces from it. By that measure, the history of programming is a ladder. On each rung, people stopped writing one thing and started writing something more abstract, while the old thing kept existing as output.

Since code-generating language models appeared (Chen et al. 2021), the obvious question has been whether they are a better autocomplete or something else. Andrej Karpathy framed neural networks as “Software 2.0” (Karpathy 2017) and, more recently, described prompting models in English as a new kind of programming (Karpathy 2025). I take a narrower and more testable position. I do not claim that English replaces programming languages. I claim that the unit a person writes is changing from code to a bundle of intent and checks, and that the environment a person works in is changing from an editor to a loop. If both hold, then the agentic loop is, in the plain historical sense, the next language and the next IDE.

2. Background

The ladder. When FORTRAN appeared in 1957, its designers faced deep scepticism that machine-generated code could approach hand-written assembly; much of their effort went into the optimiser, precisely to win that argument (Backus 1978). They won, and the pattern repeated with every later level of abstraction.

Natural language as code. The idea of programming in English is old. Jean Sammet discussed it in 1966 (Sammet 1966); Edsger Dijkstra called it foolish in the late 1970s, arguing that the precision of formal notation is a feature, not a burden (Dijkstra, n.d.). Program synthesis research pursued the goal from specifications and examples for decades (Gulwani et al. 2017), with success in narrow domains.

Agents that code. Language models trained on code reached usable accuracy on small functions in 2021 (Chen et al. 2021). Since then, agents that read a repository, edit files, run tests and iterate have been evaluated on real GitHub issues (Jimenez et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024). The productivity evidence is mixed: a controlled experiment found developers 55.8% faster on a small, well-specified task with an AI pair programmer (Peng et al. 2023), while a randomised study of experienced open-source developers on their own mature repositories found them 19% slower with early-2025 tools (Becker et al. 2025).

3. A minimal definition

I define a program, in the agentic sense, as a tuple

where is the intent, what is wanted, stated in words and examples; is a set of executable checks (tests, types, properties, linters) that a candidate implementation must pass; is the context, the repository and its conventions; and is the set of tools and interfaces the agent may use, described as data in the sense of The Interface Is Data.

An agent maps a program to code, . A classical compiler is deterministic and preserves meaning by construction. An agent does neither. It is a stochastic compiler: its output can vary between runs, and it is correct only in the weak sense that

Call the specification gap of the set of behaviours that pass but are not what meant. The whole discipline of the new language is to make this gap small: by sharpening , by strengthening , and by having a person review what remains.

Under this definition, the concepts of the familiar toolchain map onto new ones.

Table 1. The toolchain, translated. My own mapping.
Today In the agentic loop
Source file Intent, examples and checks:
Compiler Agent: , stochastic
Type checker Tests, types and properties:
Standard library Tools and interfaces:
Build configuration Repository context and conventions:
Debugger Decision log and execution trace of the agent
Code review Review of intent first, then of the diff
Editor Plan, diff and checks panes; typing as fallback

4. Four arguments

4.1 Historical. Every previous rung of the ladder was resisted on the grounds that generated output was slower, less precise or less trustworthy than what experts wrote by hand (Backus 1978). Each time, the generated output improved, the cost of writing by hand stayed the same, and the line crossed. Nothing in the current situation suggests the pattern has stopped; the objections raised today are the same three.

4.2 Structural. Brooks distinguished the essential complexity of software, deciding precisely what it must do, from its accidental complexity, the effort of expressing that decision in a particular language and toolset (Brooks 1987). Under the definition above, a person writes and , which carry the essential complexity, and the agent handles the expression, which is accidental. This is the division of labour every abstraction has aimed for, achieved at a higher level than before. Tests, long promoted as a design discipline (Beck 2002), become the main way to state that essential part.

4.3 Economic. The cost of producing a correct change has three parts: writing it, checking it, and understanding it later. Agentic coding drives the first towards zero and leaves the other two. A rational team will therefore spend its people where the cost remains, on intent, checks and review, which is exactly the shift from editor to loop that the thesis predicts. The IDE follows the work: when typing is no longer the bottleneck, an environment organised around typing is the wrong shape.

4.4 Empirical. Agents now resolve a meaningful share of real repository issues under controlled evaluation (Jimenez et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024), a task that requires reading context, editing several files and passing existing tests: the full loop of Figure 2, not autocomplete. The negative result of Becker et al. (2025) is important and I return to it in §6, but it measures an early tool generation, on large mature repositories, with developers who had little experience of the new way of working. That is close to measuring FORTRAN in 1957 with assembly experts.

5. Predictions

A position paper should be falsifiable. If the thesis is right, the following should be observed in professional software over the next few years; if they are not, it is wrong.

  • H1. Authorship shifts. The share of merged changes whose code was primarily produced by an agent keeps rising in professional repositories, measurable from commit metadata and tool logs.
  • H2. Checks grow relative to code. In human-written lines, the ratio of tests, types and specifications to implementation rises.
  • H3. Review becomes the main human cost. Time spent reviewing and specifying exceeds time spent writing code, in the same teams that adopt agents.
  • H4. Gains follow the strength of checks. Productivity gains from agents are larger where is strong (well-tested code with clear conventions) than where it is weak, other things equal. This is the most direct test of claim 3.

6. Objections

Natural language is too imprecise (Dijkstra). This is right, and it is the most important objection. But the program in §3 is not prose alone. Its precision lives in , in and in review, as it always has in teams where a person states a need and an engineer implements it. The objection becomes a design rule: wherever precision matters, state it as a check, not as a sentence.

A stochastic compiler cannot be trusted. Deterministic compilers can be trusted because their meaning-preservation can be argued once. A stochastic compiler cannot; it must be checked every time. This raises the value of and of review, and it means that for code where checks are weak and errors are costly, the old way should remain. The thesis predicts a shift in the default, not the end of hand-written code.

Developers are slower, not faster (Becker et al. 2025). If replications on strong-check repositories, with experienced users of current tools, continue to find slowdowns, H4 fails and so does much of this paper. I consider this the most likely way for me to be wrong.

Code is still the artefact that runs. Yes, as assembly still runs. The thesis does not say code disappears; it says it stops being the thing people mainly write. Like assembly, it remains the layer that can always be read, and to which the machine is held.

Literate programming tried this. Knuth argued that programs should be written for people first (Knuth 1984). Literate programming kept the person as the author of the code. The difference here is that the person is the author of the intent and the checks, and the code is derived.

7. Conclusion

Every generation of programmers was told that the next level of abstraction was a toy, and each time the toy became the language. I have argued, on purpose without hedging, that the agentic loop is the next such level: the source becomes intent plus checks, the compiler becomes a stochastic agent held to those checks, and the IDE becomes a place to steer and review. The definition makes one consequence precise. The new language is exactly as rigorous as its checks, so the craft of programming does not disappear; it moves into specification, testing and judgement. Four predictions make the claim testable. I expect to be partly wrong. I would rather be wrong in a way that can be measured.

Read next · The Interface Is Data How MCP and the agentic loop change what we call an API.

item.title: The Interface Is Data
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Agentic Coding · Part 2 of 5 · Read the whole series

Essay, October 2026. A companion to Fast AI, An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle and The Junior Colleague. All figures are my own, drawn with the code in figs.py. Where a figure uses someone else’s numbers, the caption names the source. Where the numbers are my own illustrative assumptions, the caption says so.

In short. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is usually presented as a way to give AI models access to tools. I think it does something larger. It changes what we mean by an API. A classic API is a contract that a developer reads once and then turns into code. An MCP server describes itself as data that any caller reads when it makes the call: what each tool does, what it accepts and returns, and whether it is safe to retry. The agentic loop is what made this practical, because for the first time a general client can read the description and act on it. But the idea does not need AI. A workflow engine, a form generator, a test suite or a policy gateway can read the same description. Once interfaces are data, tools can be connected as a graph of any shape, the same capability can be offered at several levels of detail, and much of the glue code between systems disappears. Pushed one step further, a tool can be found by the meaning of its description and can return not data but a program: a sub-graph of other tools, checked and run by an executor, then kept as a new tool. Programs then live inside the process, as data. MCP also has serious weaknesses: it fills the model’s context, it opens new security holes, and plain prose is a weak contract. Some of the alternatives are better for parts of the job. My conclusion is that the lasting change is not the protocol. It is the habit of publishing an interface as data and choosing, case by case, when to bind to it.

TipKey takeaways
  • An API used to be read by people and turned into code. An MCP tool is a piece of data, read by its caller at the moment of the call. The key change is not the wire format. It is when the interface is bound.
  • The idea is old; the reader is new. Self-describing services (WSDL, REST hypermedia) were proposed twenty-five years ago and mostly failed, because no general client could read the descriptions. A language model in a loop can.
  • The idea does not need AI. Of the six readers of a tool description I describe below, only one is a model.
  • Described tools form a web. A server can also be a client, so tools compose into hubs, meshes or layers. With clients and services, the adapters to write fall from to .
  • Granularity becomes a choice for the caller. One server can offer a whole capability, a few workflows, single tools and raw operations, and each caller picks its level.
  • A tool can return a program. Embed tool descriptions to find them by meaning, let a tool return a sub-graph of calls, check it and run it without a model, then store it as a new tool. The line between API, workflow and program becomes a matter of level.
  • The case against MCP is real. Tool descriptions crowd the model’s context, poisoned descriptions and prompt injection are real attacks, prose is a weak contract, and code, CLIs or typed SDKs are often simpler.
  • The SDK does not die; it moves. Explore with an agent over described tools, then compile what repeats into typed code, the step I called Fast AI.

1. The ritual of the SDK

Anyone who has connected two business systems knows the ritual. You find the documentation of the other system’s API. You read it, usually twice. You install its SDK for your language, or write a client if none exists. You map its objects to yours, handle its errors, its paging, its authentication, its rate limits. You write tests. Months later, the other side publishes version 3, and you start again.

The cost of this ritual is not in any single step. It is in the number of times we repeat it. Every pair of systems that must talk needs its own piece of glue, written by a person who has read the documentation of both. In a company with ten applications and fifty services, that is a lot of glue, and most of it does nothing more interesting than translate one shape of data into another.

For thirty years the answer has been better documentation and better code generation: WSDL in the early 2000s, then Swagger and OpenAPI, then typed client generators. They helped. But the contract was still read by a person and bound into code before the program ran. The program itself never knew what the service could do. It only knew what its developer had written down.

2. What MCP changes: the description is read at run time

MCP was published by Anthropic in November 2024 as an open standard for connecting AI applications to data and tools (Anthropic 2024). Technically it is modest. Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0. A server exposes tools (actions), resources (data to read) and prompts (reusable instructions). A client asks the server what it offers with tools/list and calls a tool with tools/call (Model Context Protocol 2025). The protocol says openly that it takes inspiration from the Language Server Protocol, which solved a similar problem between code editors and programming languages (Microsoft 2016).

What matters is in the answer to tools/list. Each tool comes back as a small piece of data: a name, a human-readable title, a description in plain words, a JSON Schema for its input, and since the June 2025 revision, an optional schema for its output and annotations: hints such as whether the tool only reads, whether it can destroy something, whether it is safe to call twice (Model Context Protocol 2025). The server can also tell the client that its list of tools has changed.

None of these fields is new on its own. JSON Schema has existed for more than fifteen years, and OpenAPI already carries descriptions. The change is when the interface is bound, and by whom. With an SDK, the binding happens when the code is written, in the head of a developer. With MCP, it happens when the call is made, inside the caller. The program no longer contains the knowledge of what the service can do. It asks.

This is why I say MCP is a way to redefine the API, at least in part. An API was a document plus a library. Here it becomes a data object that travels with the service, can be queried, filtered, logged, versioned and compared, like any other data.

3. An old dream, finally with a reader

The dream of services that describe themselves is old, and it is worth remembering why it failed.

In 2000, Roy Fielding’s dissertation defined REST and one of its constraints, hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS): a client should discover what it can do next from the links in each response, not from documentation read in advance (Fielding 2000). Almost nobody built clients that way. Around the same time, WSDL described web services in machine-readable XML (Christensen et al. 2001), and UDDI registries were supposed to let programs find services on their own. The large public UDDI registries closed in 2006.

These ideas did not fail because they were wrong. They failed because the client was missing. A description is only useful if something can read it and decide what to do. A conventional program cannot read “assigns an invoice to a budget and to the person who approves it” and work out when to call it. So in practice a developer always read the description, and the binding stayed in the code.

The agentic loop supplied that client. A language model can read a description in plain words, match it to a goal, fill in the arguments from the schema, look at the result and decide what to do next (Yao et al. 2023; Schick et al. 2023). Function calling, introduced by OpenAI in June 2023 (OpenAI 2023), gave models a structured way to do this, but each application still carried its own list of functions. Research on agents that choose among thousands of real APIs (Patil et al. 2023; Qin et al. 2024) showed both the promise and the difficulty. MCP’s contribution was to move the description out of the application and into the service, behind one protocol. Adoption was quick. By December 2025, when Anthropic gave MCP to the new Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, it counted more than 10,000 active public MCP servers (Anthropic 2025b).

4. The idea does not need AI

This is the part I find most interesting, and most often missed. Once a service publishes its interface as data, the language model becomes just one of its readers.

  • A workflow engine or a plain script can call a tool by name, with arguments checked against the schema, and never involve a model.
  • A form generator can build a screen from the input schema, so a person can call the same tool by hand.
  • A test generator can produce valid and invalid calls from the schemas and check that the outputs match the output schema.
  • A policy gateway can read the annotations and decide, for example, that destructive tools require a human approval.
  • A catalogue can index every tool in the company, with its owner, its version and how often it is used.

Seen this way, MCP is less an AI protocol than a data-driven way of building integrations. The interface is a record in a catalogue. The behaviour of the system, which tools exist, who may call them, which ones chain together, can be changed by changing data rather than code. The agentic loop is optional. The description is not.

This matters for the argument I made in Fast AI. There I argued that the large model should do the slow, exploratory work once, and that what repeats should be compiled into something fast and fixed. A data-driven interface makes that compilation easy: the recipe an agent discovered can be stored as data (call extract_invoice, then match_po, then pick_approver) and replayed by a workflow engine with no model at all.

5. A web of tools

The second consequence is structural. In MCP, the roles of client and server are not fixed: a server can itself be a client of other servers. An “invoice desk” server can expose a single tool, route_invoice, and implement it by calling an ERP server, a document server and a decision model. A gateway can collect many servers behind one catalogue and add identity, policy and logging in one place.

The first gain is simple arithmetic, the same one that motivated the Language Server Protocol. If clients must each talk to services, writing one adapter per pair costs adapters. If every client speaks one protocol and every service publishes one description, it costs . With ten clients and fifty services, that is 60 adapters instead of 500. Each adapter is real work: reading, coding, testing, and above all maintaining it when either side changes. I suspect this, more than anything AI-related, is where most of the time is saved.

The second gain is less obvious. When every tool declares the shape of what it accepts and returns, the connections between tools become something you can compute. If extract_invoice returns an object that fits the input of match_po, the two can be chained, and a planner, human or machine, can see this without reading any code. The graph of possible compositions is a by-product of the descriptions. This is what I mean by a web of tools: not a fixed integration diagram drawn by an architect, but a graph that can be queried, searched for paths, and checked for missing links.

And the graph can take whatever shape the organisation needs. A hub puts identity and policy in one place, which most companies will want for anything that touches money or personal data. A mesh lets teams connect their servers directly, with no central bottleneck. Layers stack atomic tools under composite tools, and composite tools under agents that are themselves exposed as tools. Because every node speaks the same protocol, moving from one shape to another is a matter of configuration. This is the cross-communication benefit: teams that never coordinated their APIs can still find and call each other’s tools, through one catalogue, in one format.

6. Granularity on demand

Every API designer faces the question of grain. Too fine, and callers make dozens of chatty calls to do one thing. Too coarse, and callers cannot do anything the designer did not foresee. In the SDK world, the designer picks one grain and everybody lives with it.

Described tools loosen this choice in two ways.

First, the same server can publish several levels at once. At the top, a whole capability exposed as one tool: “handle this invoice task”, implemented by an agent. Below it, a few workflows that each deliver one result. Below those, single actions. At the bottom, the raw operations of the underlying API. A strong model working on an unusual case may want the fine tools. A workflow engine wants the workflow. Another team’s agent may only want the capability. Because each level is just more data in the same catalogue, offering all four costs little. Anthropic’s advice on writing tools for agents points the same way: fewer, more meaningful tools that match how a task is really done, rather than a thin wrapper around every endpoint (Anthropic 2025e).

Second, the caller can choose how much of the description to read. This is progressive disclosure: first the names, then the descriptions of the tools that look relevant, then their full schemas, then, if needed, their documentation or code. Agent Skills apply this idea to instructions: a model sees only a skill’s name and summary until it decides the skill is relevant, and only then reads the rest (Anthropic 2025c). Tool search does the same for large tool catalogues: tools are loaded only when a search finds them (Anthropic 2025d; Gan and Sun 2025).

The numbers show why this matters. Loading every schema of a large catalogue before the first call can cost tens of thousands of tokens, which are paid on every run and push useful context out of the window. In one workflow described by Anthropic, presenting the tools as files that the agent reads only when needed reduced the tokens used from 150,000 to 2,000, a reduction of 98.7% (Anthropic 2025a). That is one example, not a benchmark, but the direction is clear: granularity is no longer only a property of the API. It is a choice made by the caller, at run time, based on what it needs.

7. Tools that return programs

So far, every tool in this essay has returned data. I want to push the idea one step further, because I think this is where the paradigm becomes really new: a tool can return a program, and that program can stay inside the process as data.

7.1 A catalogue you search by meaning

If a tool’s description is data, it can be embedded: turned into a vector by the same kind of model used for semantic search (Reimers and Gurevych 2019). The catalogue then becomes a space in which tools that do similar things sit close together. A question, from a person, an agent or another tool, lands somewhere in that space, and its nearest neighbours are the few tools worth reading.

None of this is speculative. ToolLLM and Gorilla used a retriever to pick a handful of APIs out of thousands (Qin et al. 2024; Patil et al. 2023), and the tool search in current agent platforms works the same way (Anthropic 2025d; Gan and Sun 2025). ToolkenGPT goes further and gives each tool its own token embedding inside the model, so that calling a tool is no different from predicting a word (Hao et al. 2023).

Embeddings give the web of §5 a second kind of edge. Schema edges say which tools can be chained, because one’s output fits another’s input. Embedding distance says which tools are about the same thing. Together they are enough to propose a plan without anyone drawing it.

7.2 A tool whose result is a sub-graph

Now the step that interests me most. Nothing in the idea of a tool requires its result to be plain data. A tool can return a small graph of other tool calls, with the arguments of each node wired to the outputs of the others.

In Figure 10, plan_invoice_routing does not do the work. It returns the recipe: extract the invoice; then, in parallel, match the purchase order and fetch the supplier’s rules; then pick the approver; then notify them. An executor, which is ordinary code, checks the graph before running anything: every tool exists, every reference fits the schema it feeds, there is no cycle, the policy gateway accepts every node, and the whole stays within its limits. Then it runs the graph, with no model in the loop.

Research on agents points the same way. ReWOO separates planning from execution: the model writes the whole plan once, instead of reasoning again after every observation (Xu et al. 2023). LLMCompiler has the model emit a graph of function calls with their dependencies and runs the independent calls in parallel, which made runs faster and cheaper than step-by-step reasoning (Kim et al. 2024). Code mode and programmatic tool calling let the model write the plan as code (Varda and Pai 2025; Anthropic 2025d).

What changes in my proposal is who returns the plan. It need not be the model in the loop. It can be a tool like any other: written by a team, generated by a model and reviewed once, or retrieved from storage. The plan stops being a private thought of the agent and becomes part of the interface.

7.3 Programs inside programs

Since a node of a returned graph is just a tool call, it can itself be a tool that returns a graph.

This gives the multiple levels of detail of §6 almost for free. Nobody has to design the levels in advance: each one expands only when it is reached, and only as far as needed. A caller that trusts route_invoice treats it as one step. A caller that must audit it can ask for the graph and inspect every level. The executor needs two limits to make sure the expansion ends: a maximum depth and a budget of calls.

7.4 Keeping the programs

The last step closes the loop with Fast AI. A returned graph is data. It can be logged, compared with yesterday’s, reviewed by a person, signed, versioned and stored. Once stored with a description, it is itself a tool: it gets embedded in the same catalogue, and the next search for “who must approve this supplier invoice?” finds the stored program before anything has to plan.

Voyager, an agent that played Minecraft, worked this way: it stored every skill it learned as a program, indexed it by an embedding of its description, retrieved it when a similar task came up, and built new skills from old ones (Wang et al. 2023). Models that write their own tools and reuse them follow the same pattern (Cai et al. 2024).

In a company, the same mechanism means that the programs which run the business live inside the process, as data you can inspect, rather than hidden in the code of each application or worked out again by an agent every morning. This is what I mean by embedding programs in the process. The process is a graph of tools. Some tools return graphs. Those graphs can be kept and become tools. The difference between an API, a workflow and a program becomes a matter of level, not of kind. Programmers will recognise an old idea from Lisp, where code and data share one form. Here, the shared form is the tool description.

7.5 What it costs

A tool that returns a program is a tool that returns code, and everything §8.1 says about poisoned descriptions applies with more force. The executor must treat every returned graph as untrusted. It should run only tools from an allowed list, check every reference against its schema, apply the policy to every node and not only to the first, enforce the limits, and never let a graph call a tool its caller could not call directly. Debugging is harder too: a failure can sit three levels down, in a graph nobody wrote by hand, so every expansion must be logged with where it came from. Finally, there is no standard. MCP has no “graph” result type, so today this is a convention on top of the protocol, or a job for a workflow engine. A shared format for returned plans would, I think, be one of the most useful next steps for the ecosystem.

8. The case against MCP

So far I have made the case for. It would be dishonest to stop there. MCP has drawn serious criticism, much of it fair, and for several jobs there are better options.

8.1 Five objections

It is a wrapper over APIs that already exist. Many MCP servers are thin layers over a REST API that already had an OpenAPI description. Adding a protocol, a server process and a new failure point to say the same thing again is not obviously progress. Critics argue that a model that can read OpenAPI, or a --help page, does not need MCP at all (Ronacher 2025).

It crowds the model’s context. Every tool description an agent loads costs tokens on every call, and accuracy in choosing the right tool falls as the list grows (Gan and Sun 2025). In the paper I analysed in The Junior Colleague, each task offered 68 tools, 31 of them near-duplicates of the core ones, precisely because large, messy catalogues are what agents face in practice (Zhu et al. 2026). Progressive disclosure helps, but it is extra machinery that the protocol did not originally provide.

It opens new security holes. A tool description is text that the model reads and trusts. A malicious or compromised server can hide instructions in it, a tool-poisoning attack (Invariant Labs 2025). Any tool that returns content from the outside world can carry an indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al. 2023). Simon Willison named the dangerous combination the lethal trifecta: an agent with access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to send data out (Willison 2025). Connecting many MCP servers to one agent makes that combination easy to assemble by accident. Surveys of the MCP ecosystem list these and other threats, such as name collisions between servers and installers that cannot be verified (Hou et al. 2025). The specification itself warns that annotations are hints and should not be trusted from an unknown server (Model Context Protocol 2025).

Prose is a weak contract. A schema says that amount_chf is a number. It does not say whether it includes VAT, whether calling the tool twice creates two approvals, or what happens if the budget is closed. A typed SDK does not say this either, but it is usually paired with a developer who read the documentation and wrote tests. When the reader is a model, the description is the documentation, and its gaps become errors at run time instead of questions at design time. Versioning is also weaker: a server can change its tools between two calls.

It is slower and less predictable than a function call. An agent that reads descriptions, reasons and then calls is orders of magnitude slower and more expensive than compiled code calling a library, and it may take a different path on the same input. For processes that run ten thousand times a day, this is the wrong trade, as I argued in Fast AI.

8.2 The alternatives

  • OpenAPI plus function calling. If a service already has a good OpenAPI description, it can be turned into function definitions for a model with no new protocol (OpenAPI Initiative 2021; OpenAI 2023). This keeps one source of truth and the existing tooling for authentication, gateways and testing.
  • Code as the interface. Instead of asking the model to call tools one at a time, let it write a short program against a typed API and run it in a sandbox. Research found that agents acting through code solved more tasks than agents emitting JSON calls (Wang et al. 2024). Cloudflare’s Code Mode turns MCP tools into a TypeScript API for exactly this reason (Varda and Pai 2025), and Anthropic’s code-execution approach does the same with files (Anthropic 2025a). In this view, the SDK comes back, but its reader is now a model.
  • Command-line tools and skills. A well-made CLI already describes itself through --help, composes through pipes, and is something models have seen countless times in training. Paired with short instruction files that are read on demand (Anthropic 2025c), it covers much of what developers use MCP for, with no server to run (Ronacher 2025).
  • Agent-to-agent protocols. When the thing on the other side is itself an agent with its own judgement, a protocol for tasks between peers, such as Google’s A2A, fits better than a list of tools (Google 2025; Ehtesham et al. 2025).
  • Typed SDKs and RPC. For hot paths, nothing beats a compiled call with types checked before the program runs.
  • GraphQL. Its introspection already lets a client ask what a service offers and choose exactly the fields it needs (GraphQL Foundation 2021). It solved part of the granularity problem years ago, for data.

8.3 My reading

Most of these alternatives share MCP’s core idea: the interface is described in a form the caller reads, and the binding happens later than it used to. Code mode reads MCP descriptions and generates an SDK from them. Skills are descriptions in files. A2A publishes “agent cards”. Even the critics who say “just use the CLI” are relying on --help, a self-description read at run time.

So I do not think the lasting change is MCP the wire format. It may be replaced, merged with other protocols, or survive mainly as an internal standard behind gateways. The lasting change is the practice: publish every interface as data, rich enough for a model and precise enough for a machine, and let each caller decide when to bind to it. MCP is, for now, the most widely adopted way to do that, and its governance under a neutral foundation makes it a reasonable bet. But the objections in §8.1 are about real costs, and the right answer to several of them is to use something else for that part of the job.

9. Where the SDK survives

Back to the original question: does this redefine the API and the SDK “to an extent” or “completely”? My answer is: completely at the edges, not in the core.

At the edges, where integration happens, where a call is made rarely or differs every time, where a team needs to find and use another team’s capability, the described interface wins. It is cheaper to build, easier to discover and works for model and script alike. Here I expect hand-written SDKs to become rare.

In the core, where the same call runs thousands of times a day, the binding should happen early again: a typed client, a fixed recipe, a small decision model like the one in The Junior Colleague. The difference from before is where that code comes from. It does not need to start from a developer reading documentation. It can be generated from the same descriptions, or compiled from a path that an agent found and that people reviewed. The SDK becomes an output of the described interface, not its source.

10. What would prove me wrong

I would change my mind if:

  • tool descriptions stayed so unreliable that every serious integration still needed a person to read the documentation and write tests by hand, so the run-time binding saved nothing;
  • the security problems of §8.1 proved impossible to contain at reasonable cost, so that companies kept MCP to demos and read-only tools;
  • returned programs proved harder to secure, debug and govern than the hand-written code they replace;
  • the token cost of descriptions kept growing faster than the techniques that load them on demand;
  • integration time and maintenance, measured in real companies over a few years, did not fall for teams that publish their interfaces as data compared with teams that do not.

The last one is the real test, and it can be measured.

11. Conclusion

For decades, an API was a promise written for people. A developer read it, understood it, and turned it into code that was frozen until the next release. MCP and the agentic loop make a different arrangement possible: the promise is written as data, travels with the service, and is read by whoever calls it, at the moment of the call.

That one shift has several consequences. The caller no longer needs AI to benefit. Tools can be connected into a web of whatever shape suits the organisation, with far less glue. The same capability can be offered at several levels of detail, and each caller chooses how much to read. Tools can be found by meaning, and can return programs that are checked, run and kept as new tools, so the logic of a process lives inside it as data. And the expensive, exploratory work of figuring out how to combine tools can be done once by an agent, then compiled into something fast.

MCP may not be the protocol we use in ten years. Its weaknesses are real, and some of its alternatives are better at parts of the job. But I think the habit it is spreading will remain: an interface is not only something we read. It is data.
